newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian government reopens contact with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian government reopens contact with rebels.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori's government renewed talks on Friday with Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages in Lima in the hope of negotiating a peaceful solution to the 24-day-old crisis.
Government negotiator Domingo Palermo arranged a second face-to-face meeting with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini for the weekend.
But he insisted the government would accept nothing short of the complete release of all the remaining captives at the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.

"My goal is to free the 74 hostages in their entirety, in good health and as quickly as possible," Palermo told foreign correspondents who witnessed his four-minute, walkie-talkie conversation with the guerrilla leader.
Palermo and Cerpa were polite and gentlemanly but carefully measured in their contact, which broke a stalemate that has lasted since the last release of hostages on New Year's Day.
"How are you? It's a pleasure to hear you, Mr. Cerpa," Palermo said. "At your service, minister," replied Cerpa, before quipping: "Here we are, and we're not going anywhere."
"I congratulate you for your good sense of humour," responded Palermo, grinning.
Cerpa agreed to allow Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani to return to the residence on Sunday to celebrate Mass with the hostages.
Palermo also spoke by telephone with Fujimori during his nearly three-hour meeting with correspondents from Reuters, the Italian news agency ANSA, Agence France Presse and Mexican TV channel ECO.
It was the government negotiator's first contact with the media since MRTA rebels stormed the residence during a Dec. 17 cocktail party.
Fujimori hailed the talk with Cerpa as a "good sign" that raised "hopeful prospects" of a bloodless end to the crisis.
"We have established a bridge via today's radio contact," he told local radio station Radio Programas.
Palermo has met Cerpa once face-to-face on Dec. 28 when he won the release of 20 hostages, and had also been in contact via short, handwritten messages.

"I am the contact, not the negotiator, though you could say it is the same thing," he told the correspondents. Palermo heads a government crisis mini-team that also includes Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi, Energy Minister Daniel Hokama and Economy Minister Jorge Camet.

A senior government source added that a provisional "guarantor committee" was being set up to supervise a possible negotiated end. The committee would consist of members of the government and "two or three very strong institutions or countries," the source said.

Neither Palermo nor other government sources would give more details on the proposal -- floated on Thursday by Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi and confirmed on Friday by Fujimori -- that the rebels may be allowed to leave the country if they lay down arms and release the captives.
The source revealed that the trickle of releases of hostages up to New Year's Day had all been carefully negotiated by the government and the rebels.

Part of the government strategy in the standoff has been to establish a psychological profile of Cerpa to facilitate talks with him, the source added. "We have seen that he's the classic 'union leader' type ... someone who goes to see his boss to ask for a raise of $100 but knowing he will only receive $50 or less," the source said.
"At the beginning he was very aggressive, but now he has calmed down a lot," the source added.
